text: In this lesson, what does the European term “New World” refer to?
answers: The Americas
The Asian trading regions Europeans hoped to reach
The European kingdoms sponsoring ocean voyages
The African ports used on routes toward Asia
solution: Europeans used “New World” for the Americas. Indigenous peoples had lived there long before these European voyages.
hint: Think about whose point of view made these lands seem “new.”
source: NPS: Prelude to Jamestown; TCI published topic outline

text: Why did many European merchants support voyages in the late 1400s?
answers: They hoped to find profitable sea routes to Asian goods
They wanted to avoid buying or selling goods abroad
They were certain a western sea route to Asia was already mapped
They wanted to bring Asian goods to the Americas without selling them
solution: Demand for Asian goods, including spices and silk, encouraged the search for sea routes that could make trade more profitable.
hint: Separate a reason for traveling from a tool used during travel.
source: NPS: Prelude to Jamestown; TCI published topic outline

text: Which period best fits the start of the European voyages studied in this lesson?
answers: The late 1400s
The late 1600s, after the English colonies had expanded
The late 1700s, during the American Revolution
The late 1800s, during westward railroad expansion
solution: This lesson focuses on European ocean voyages expanding from the late 1400s into the 1500s.
hint: Columbus’s Atlantic crossing in 1492 belongs to this period.
source: NPS: Prelude to Jamestown; TCI published topic outline

text: Columbus sailed west across the Atlantic in 1492 hoping to reach which trading region?
answers: Asia
The Americas, which he already knew were between Europe and Asia
The English colonies that already existed on the Atlantic coast
The gold mines of Mexico that he had previously visited
solution: Columbus hoped to reach Asia by sailing west for Spain. He reached islands in the Americas instead.
hint: Distinguish the destination he hoped for from the place he actually reached.
source: NPS: Prelude to Jamestown; TCI published topic outline

text: A teammate writes, “The Americas had no people until Europeans arrived.” Which correction is accurate?
answers: Indigenous peoples already had communities and cultures there
Indigenous communities began only after European governments formed them
European mapmakers named places before anyone could settle there
Indigenous peoples lived there but had no farms or trading networks
solution: The Americas were already home to many Indigenous peoples. European arrival was not the beginning of American history.
hint: The name “New World” describes a European perspective, not an empty place.
source: NPS: Prelude to Jamestown; TCI published topic outline

text: Which list contains European countries involved in the era’s ocean exploration?
answers: Spain, Portugal, England, and France
Spain, China, and the Aztec Empire
England, the Inca Empire, and Japan
France, Antarctica, and the Pacific Ocean
solution: Spain, Portugal, England, and France sponsored European exploration; the Netherlands also became involved. The other lists mix countries with Indigenous empires or geographic features.
hint: Look for a list made entirely of European countries.
source: NPS: Prelude to Jamestown; TCI published topic outline

text: How are “how Europeans traveled” and “why Europeans traveled” different questions?
answers: “How” asks about methods and tools; “why” asks about motives
“How” asks about desired wealth; “why” asks about instruments and routes
Both ask only about the cargo carried back to Europe
Both ask only about the countries that paid for the voyage
solution: Ships and navigation tools help explain how voyages happened. Trade, power, and religion help explain why people supported them.
hint: A compass is a method; the hope of profit is a motive.
source: NPS: Prelude to Jamestown; TCI published topic outline

text: Which explanation best connects European demand with exploration?
answers: Wanting Asian goods encouraged investment in sea voyages
European demand for Asian goods began only after tobacco reached Europe
Navigation instruments caused merchants to stop seeking trade profits
Existing overland trade made new sea routes unnecessary for merchants
solution: Demand for goods helped motivate voyages. Navigation tools made travel more possible, but tools alone do not explain the desire to trade.
hint: Connect what merchants wanted with the journeys they were willing to fund.
source: NPS: Prelude to Jamestown; TCI published topic outline

text: Which instrument used the angle of the sun or stars to help sailors estimate latitude?
answers: An astrolabe
A magnetic compass that indicated a ship’s heading
A map showing coastlines and possible sailing routes
A ship’s log recording cargo and daily voyage events
solution: An astrolabe helped measure the angle of a visible heavenly body. Sailors could use that information to estimate latitude.
hint: Latitude means position north or south of the equator.
source: NPS: Navigating the Atlantic World

text: Far from shore, a sailor cannot see familiar hills or buildings. What navigation problem does this create?
answers: Landmarks can no longer guide the ship’s position
Magnetic north changes into the ship’s current latitude
Knowing the direction of travel gives an exact location
The nearest coast must match every feature on the chart
solution: On the open ocean, familiar land features are missing. Sailors needed instruments, observations, and charts to navigate.
hint: What kinds of clues disappear when land is out of sight?
source: NPS: Navigating the Atlantic World

text: Which pairing correctly distinguishes two navigation tools?
answers: Astrolabe: latitude clues; compass: direction
Astrolabe: compass direction; compass: latitude clues
Astrolabe: east–west position; compass: exact distance from shore
Astrolabe: sailing speed; compass: the sun’s height
solution: An astrolabe used sky angles to help estimate latitude. A compass helped sailors determine direction. Neither was a modern GPS.
hint: Ask whether the tool answers “how far north?” or “which way?”
source: NPS: Navigating the Atlantic World

text: A squadmate says an astrolabe instantly showed a ship’s exact location on a screen. What is the best correction?
answers: It measured sky angles to help estimate latitude, not a screen location
It pointed toward magnetic north so sailors could steer a heading
It gave exact east–west position without needing sky observations
It automatically drew coastlines that sailors had not yet visited
solution: An astrolabe was an observing instrument, not an electronic location system. Position estimates required observations and calculations.
hint: Think of observing the sky rather than receiving a satellite signal.
source: NPS: Navigating the Atlantic World

text: Clouds hide the sun and stars. Which task becomes harder with an astrolabe?
answers: Taking a useful sky-angle observation
Following a heading with a magnetic compass
Comparing a drawn coastline with a written voyage record
Reading the name of a port already shown on a chart
solution: An astrolabe depends on observing the sun or stars. A cloudy sky can prevent the needed sighting.
hint: Which tool needs a view of the sky?
source: NPS: Navigating the Atlantic World

text: Why did navigation tools matter for long ocean crossings?
answers: They supplied clues when sailors lacked familiar land features
They guaranteed arrival because a heading is the same as a location
They made maps unnecessary once sailors learned the direction north
They were mainly used to decide which country should claim the land
solution: Instruments and maps helped sailors navigate beyond familiar coasts. They reduced some uncertainty without removing storms, shortages, or mistakes.
hint: A useful tool can reduce a risk without eliminating every danger.
source: NPS: Navigating the Atlantic World

text: What does latitude describe?
answers: How far north or south a place is from the equator
How expensive a ship’s cargo is
The direction the wind must blow
How far east or west a place is from a reference line
solution: Latitude measures north–south position relative to the equator. East–west position is longitude.
hint: Picture the equator and locations above or below it.
source: NPS: Navigating the Atlantic World

text: An exhibit shows an astrolabe and a model sailing ship. Which label best connects them?
answers: Technology used to make ocean travel possible
Products introduced to Europe from Indigenous American farming
Motive symbols showing that religious conversion was the only goal
Evidence that sailors already knew every coastline before departure
solution: Ships provided transportation; instruments helped sailors navigate. These are methods of travel rather than crops or motives.
hint: Classify objects by what people used them to do.
source: NPS: Navigating the Atlantic World

text: What did a magnetic compass mainly help a sailor determine?
answers: Direction
The ship’s exact latitude and longitude together
The number of miles remaining before reaching a port
The depth of water under the ship’s hull
solution: A compass’s magnetic needle indicates north and helps a sailor keep a heading. It does not directly measure depth, age, or prices.
hint: A compass answers “which way?”
source: NPS: Navigating the Atlantic World

text: The sky is cloudy and no stars are visible. Which tool can still help a sailor keep a direction?
answers: A magnetic compass
An astrolabe measuring the angle of a star hidden by clouds
A royal flag showing which country funded the voyage
A cargo record showing the prices of the goods aboard
solution: A compass uses magnetism rather than a clear view of the stars. It remains useful when clouds block sky observations.
hint: Choose the tool that does not need visible heavenly bodies.
source: NPS: Navigating the Atlantic World

text: A map’s compass rose shows north at the top. Which direction is to the right?
answers: East
West
South
North
solution: With north at the top of this compass rose, east is on the right, south at the bottom, and west on the left.
hint: Use the order north, east, south, west around the compass rose.
source: NPS: Navigating the Atlantic World

text: A navigator knows the ship is heading west. What can a compass alone NOT tell the navigator?
answers: The ship’s exact location in the ocean
A reference direction for north
Whether the heading is generally west
The direction opposite east
solution: Knowing a direction is not the same as knowing a location. A compass provides a heading reference, not an exact position.
hint: Many ships can face west while being in very different places.
source: NPS: Navigating the Atlantic World

text: Which statement correctly compares a compass with an astrolabe?
answers: A compass uses magnetism; an astrolabe uses sky observations
A compass estimates latitude; an astrolabe points toward magnetic north
Both instruments show exact position without a map or calculations
A compass needs a clear sky; an astrolabe works by magnetism
solution: These instruments provided different clues. The compass indicated direction; sky observations with an astrolabe helped estimate latitude.
hint: Think about what each instrument responds to.
source: NPS: Navigating the Atlantic World

text: Why might a captain use a compass AND a map?
answers: The compass gives a direction while the map shows places and routes
The compass shows the route while the map points toward magnetic north
Both tools supply exact position, so either one alone is always enough
The map supplies the wind, while the compass shows where cargo was grown
solution: A map and compass answer different questions. A sailor can compare a heading with the route and land features shown on a map.
hint: Tools can complement one another without doing the same job.
source: NPS: Navigating the Atlantic World

text: Which direction is opposite north?
answers: South
East
West
Northeast
solution: North and south are opposite directions. East and west are another opposite pair.
hint: Think of the bottom of a compass rose with north at the top.
source: NPS: Navigating the Atlantic World

text: An artifact has a turning magnetic needle and direction markings. What is its most likely use?
answers: Helping sailors keep a heading
Helping sailors estimate latitude by measuring a sky angle
Helping historians identify the ruler who claimed a coastline
Helping traders measure the value of American crops in Europe
solution: A needle and direction markings support identifying a compass used for navigation. They do not support claims about religion or crop amounts.
hint: Use the object’s features as evidence of its function.
source: NPS: Navigating the Atlantic World

text: What information is a navigation map designed to show?
answers: Locations of land, water, and possible routes
The personal motives of every sailor who followed a route
The exact weather at each point for every future voyage
The amount of profit guaranteed by reaching each port
solution: Maps represent places and spatial relationships. They can help sailors plan routes and identify coasts or landing places.
hint: A map represents where things are, rather than every fact about them.
source: NPS: Navigating the Atlantic World; Prelude to Jamestown

text: A returning sailor reports a coastline that earlier charts left out. What should a mapmaker do?
answers: Compare the report with other evidence and revise the map if supported
Keep the chart unchanged because royal approval makes it accurate
Accept the report as proof that every older source is useless
Label the new coast as uninhabited simply because it was not mapped
solution: New observations can improve maps, but comparing sources helps check accuracy. An early chart could be useful while still incomplete.
hint: New evidence can improve a model without making every old detail wrong.
source: NPS: Navigating the Atlantic World; Prelude to Jamestown

text: A teammate claims every European map in 1492 showed the Americas accurately. What is the best correction?
answers: Maps reflected limited information and could contain errors
Royal approval made every European map complete before ships sailed
Using a compass meant mapmakers could already draw all American coasts
Trade with Asia meant European sailors had already charted every Atlantic island
solution: Mapmakers worked with the information available to them. European knowledge of Atlantic routes and American coastlines developed through voyages.
hint: A map can include only the information its makers have gathered or inferred.
source: NPS: Navigating the Atlantic World; Prelude to Jamestown

text: A sketch map has a harbor west of an island. With north at the top, where is the harbor?
answers: To the left of the island
To the right of the island
Directly above the island
Directly below the island
solution: When north is at the top, west is to the left. The compass rose supplies the needed orientation.
hint: Use the map’s stated orientation, not a guess about a real coast.
source: NPS: Navigating the Atlantic World; Prelude to Jamestown

text: What is the main difference between a ship’s log and a map?
answers: A log records voyage events; a map represents places and routes
A log represents places; a map records each day’s events aboard ship
A log proves every sailor’s motive; a map proves the land was empty
A log gives only directions; a map gives only the amount of trade profit
solution: Written voyage records and maps preserve different kinds of information. Both can help historians understand a journey.
hint: One is a record of what happened; the other shows spatial relationships.
source: NPS: Navigating the Atlantic World; Prelude to Jamestown

text: Why should historians compare a voyage map with the ship’s written records?
answers: Different sources can support or challenge the same route claim
Using two sources guarantees every missing detail can be filled in
A map is always more reliable than a log, regardless of its evidence
A written record always cancels any conflicting observation on a map
solution: Comparing sources helps check interpretations and notice missing or conflicting information. Neither a map nor a log is automatically perfect.
hint: Stronger explanations use relevant evidence from more than one source.
source: NPS: Navigating the Atlantic World; Prelude to Jamestown

text: Which object belongs with an astrolabe and compass in a navigation display?
answers: A chart showing a coastline and sailing route
A royal flag displaying the ruler who supported a voyage
A bundle of tobacco intended for sale in a European port
A Bible carried for Christian religious teaching aboard a ship
solution: The chart helps sailors locate places and plan a route. The other objects relate to products or rulers rather than navigation.
hint: Group objects by their job, rather than their age or color.
source: NPS: Navigating the Atlantic World; Prelude to Jamestown

text: An old map leaves a large ocean area blank. What is the most cautious interpretation?
answers: The mapmaker may have lacked reliable information about that area
No Indigenous community could have known the area before it was mapped
The area contained no land because the map had no land symbol there
Every sailor knew the area but mapmakers always left known places blank
solution: A blank space can show a limit in a particular mapmaker’s knowledge. It does not prove the place was empty or unknown to everyone.
hint: Separate a limit in one source from a claim about the whole world.
source: NPS: Navigating the Atlantic World; Prelude to Jamestown

text: In this lesson, what is a nation-state?
answers: A country with its own government and territory
A trading ship that travels between several different countries
A territory shared by all European rulers with no separate government
A community defined only by one cargo product rather than government
solution: A nation-state has political authority over a territory. European rulers wanted to strengthen their countries through overseas expansion.
hint: This word describes a political country, not an object on a ship.
source: NPS: When Worlds Collide; Significance of Spanish Colonial Missions

text: Why might an explorer carry a flag bearing a European ruler’s symbols?
answers: To represent that ruler and make a claim to territory
To measure latitude from the stars
To show that every Indigenous nation agreed with the claim
To prove that the land had no inhabitants
solution: Flags could symbolize a ruler’s claimed authority. Raising one did not establish that existing inhabitants accepted the claim.
hint: A flag can show who is making a claim without proving everyone accepts it.
source: NPS: When Worlds Collide; Significance of Spanish Colonial Missions

text: Why did European rulers compete to claim land across the Atlantic?
answers: Territory and resources could increase their power and wealth
Claiming distant land meant rulers no longer needed trade or resources
Every ruler agreed that claiming land would end rivalry among countries
European claims meant Indigenous communities voluntarily changed rulers
solution: Rulers sought resources, influence, and power. Competition among countries helped encourage exploration and colonization.
hint: Think about what a ruler hoped their country would gain.
source: NPS: When Worlds Collide; Significance of Spanish Colonial Missions

text: A European journal calls a place “newly discovered,” but Indigenous families already live there. Which statement includes both perspectives?
answers: It was new to those visitors, not a place without history or people
A European name erased the names and histories already used by local people
The families’ presence meant no European could ever be unfamiliar with the place
A journal’s claim establishes Indigenous agreement with European control
solution: A European visitor’s description reflects that visitor’s knowledge. Indigenous peoples already had their own homes, names, histories, and political communities.
hint: Ask “new to whom?” before accepting a discovery claim.
source: NPS: When Worlds Collide; Significance of Spanish Colonial Missions

text: A teammate says, “Planting a flag means the land was freely given to that ruler.” What is the best response?
answers: A flag shows a claim, not proof of Indigenous agreement
Flags are legal signatures by every nearby person
A flag always means land was empty
Every country used one shared flag
solution: Claiming authority and receiving agreement are different things. European land claims often conflicted with Indigenous peoples’ sovereignty and rights.
hint: Do not turn evidence of a claim into evidence of consent.
source: NPS: When Worlds Collide; Significance of Spanish Colonial Missions

text: Which goal is mainly about political power?
answers: Claiming territory for a ruler
Using the angle of the sun to estimate a ship’s latitude
Using a compass and chart to follow a sailing route
Recording the kinds of food carried home from a voyage
solution: Claiming territory concerns authority and control. Instruments concern how to travel; food cargo concerns products.
hint: Identify the goal about governing or controlling land.
source: NPS: When Worlds Collide; Significance of Spanish Colonial Missions

text: Which pairing best matches a shipboard object with a motive?
answers: Royal banner → territorial power
Compass → desire to gain new territory
Astrolabe → desire to spread Christianity
Corn → authority to govern an inhabited coastline
solution: A royal banner can represent a ruler and territorial claim. Tools help with travel; crops do not measure location.
hint: Match a symbol of a ruler with a goal involving that ruler.
source: NPS: When Worlds Collide; Significance of Spanish Colonial Missions

text: Which explanation avoids treating European expansion as a benefit for everyone?
answers: It could enrich rulers while taking land and harming Indigenous communities
Every land claim improved life equally for all people
Only rulers had cultures worth studying
A successful voyage proves no one was harmed
solution: The consequences depended on whose experience is considered. European gains could come alongside Indigenous land loss, violence, and coercion.
hint: Compare who gained power with who could lose land or freedom.
source: NPS: When Worlds Collide; Significance of Spanish Colonial Missions

text: Which belief system did many European missionaries seek to spread in the Americas?
answers: Christianity
Religious beliefs they learned only after arriving in the Americas
The belief that every Indigenous religion should remain unchanged
The belief that religion and European expansion were never connected
solution: European missionaries sought to spread Christianity. Religion was one motive for expansion, alongside wealth and political power.
hint: Choose a religion, rather than a technology or economic activity.
source: NPS: Significance of Spanish Colonial Missions

text: Which shipboard object most directly suggests Christian religious activity?
answers: A Bible
An astrolabe used for observations during an ocean crossing
A royal banner used to represent a European government
A written cargo list used to track the amount of silver
solution: A Bible is a Christian religious text. Its presence can support a religious connection, although it cannot prove everyone aboard shared the same motive.
hint: Look for an object used in religious teaching or worship.
source: NPS: Significance of Spanish Colonial Missions

text: Why did Catholic rulers support priests traveling to the Americas?
answers: They wanted to spread the Catholic Christian faith
They believed priests were needed mainly to draw more accurate coastlines
They expected missionaries to prevent every possible trading loss
They wanted missionaries to make Indigenous beliefs the official religion in Europe
solution: Supporting missionaries could serve a ruler’s religious goals. It was different from using instruments to navigate or searching for precious metals.
hint: Connect a ruler’s religious support with conversion rather than location or cargo.
source: NPS: Significance of Spanish Colonial Missions

text: An archaeologist finds one Bible in a shipwreck. Which conclusion is best supported?
answers: Christian religious materials were carried on that ship
Every person aboard traveled only for religion
The ship could not have carried trade goods
Every Indigenous person accepted the visitors’ religion
solution: The artifact supports the presence of Christian materials. One object cannot establish every traveler’s belief or rule out other purposes.
hint: Make the smallest claim supported by the evidence you have.
source: NPS: Significance of Spanish Colonial Missions

text: How are seeking gold and sending missionaries different motives?
answers: One seeks wealth; the other seeks to spread religious beliefs
Both are mainly methods for finding a safe route across the Atlantic
Both prove every sailor aboard had one identical personal reason
Sending missionaries is an economic goal while seeking gold is religious
solution: Precious metals relate to wealth. Missionary activity relates to spreading faith. A voyage could involve more than one motive.
hint: Name the goal of each action before comparing them.
source: NPS: Significance of Spanish Colonial Missions

text: Which statement treats religious conversion in its historical context?
answers: Missionaries sought converts, but Indigenous peoples already had beliefs and did not all freely accept conversion
Indigenous peoples had no beliefs before missionaries arrived
Carrying a Bible proves every conversion was voluntary
All Europeans and Indigenous peoples practiced one identical religion
solution: Indigenous peoples had varied religious traditions. Describing missionary goals does not mean conversion was universal, freely chosen, or harmless.
hint: A visitor’s goal does not tell you how every community responded.
source: NPS: Significance of Spanish Colonial Missions

text: Which entry belongs in the “religious motives” column?
answers: Teaching Christianity to seek converts
Using a royal banner to claim land for a European ruler
Seeking profits by selling American crops in European markets
Taking sky observations to estimate a ship’s latitude
solution: Seeking converts is a religious goal. The other actions concern navigation, commerce, or maps.
hint: Ask which action is about spreading beliefs.
source: NPS: Significance of Spanish Colonial Missions

text: A voyage carries a Bible, trade goods, and a royal banner. Which explanation fits best?
answers: Religious, economic, and political purposes could overlap
The Bible proves no one cared about trade
The goods prove there was no religious activity
The banner proves the entire crew shared one personal goal
solution: European expansion often combined religion, trade, and power. Different objects can support different purposes without proving every person’s intentions.
hint: More than one motive can be present in the same voyage.
source: NPS: Significance of Spanish Colonial Missions

text: Which pair of materials did European rulers value as precious metals?
answers: Gold and silver
Gold and tobacco sold as American crops
Silver and spices used as navigation instruments
Silk and potatoes carried as food plants
solution: Gold and silver were valued as wealth. Seeking them was an economic motive rather than a method of navigation.
hint: Choose metals, rather than foods or ordinary construction materials.
source: NPS: Prelude to Jamestown; When Worlds Collide

text: Why could merchants profit from a new sea route to Asian spices?
answers: They hoped to obtain valuable goods through more direct trade
A new route would remove all costs and every risk from overseas trade
Merchants could profit only if Europeans had never wanted spices before
Asian goods would have no sale value once a sea route reached their source
solution: European demand for Asian goods encouraged more direct trade routes. Merchants hoped sales would exceed the costs and risks of the voyages.
hint: Connect demand for goods with the possibility of earning money.
source: NPS: Prelude to Jamestown; When Worlds Collide

text: Which distinction correctly separates a motive from a tool?
answers: Seeking silver is a motive; using an astrolabe is a method
Using a compass is a motive; earning trade profits is a navigation method
Seeking gold is a navigation tool; sailing a route is a religious goal
Carrying a royal flag always proves profit was the voyage’s only motive
solution: The wish to gain wealth explains why someone supports a voyage. An astrolabe helps explain how sailors navigate it.
hint: Ask whether each item is a desired result or a way of traveling.
source: NPS: Prelude to Jamestown; When Worlds Collide

text: A merchant funds a voyage hoping to sell its cargo for more than the voyage costs. What is the main motive?
answers: Profit
Measuring the ship’s latitude from the stars
Converting people to a religious faith
Recording the locations of unfamiliar coastlines
solution: The merchant expects a financial gain from trade. That is an economic motive, even if others on the voyage have additional goals.
hint: Follow what this particular merchant hopes to gain.
source: NPS: Prelude to Jamestown; When Worlds Collide

text: A teammate says, “Wealth meant only gold; crops could never earn money.” Which correction is strongest?
answers: Valuable crops and trade goods could also produce profits
Trade profits were possible only from cargo containing gold and silver
Crop sales were religious activity rather than economic activity
Only crops kept for the grower’s own meals could provide trade income
solution: Wealth could come from trade and crop sales as well as precious metals. Tobacco exports are one example of a profitable product.
hint: Something does not need to be metal to have a market value.
source: NPS: Prelude to Jamestown; When Worlds Collide

text: A voyage record describes large payments for silver cargo. What can it most directly support?
answers: The cargo had economic value to the people involved
The ship’s compass was accurate
Every worker involved was treated fairly
The whole crew traveled only to convert people
solution: Payments for silver support an economic connection. They do not establish navigation accuracy, fair treatment, or everyone’s private motives.
hint: Match the conclusion to the kind of evidence in the record.
source: NPS: Prelude to Jamestown; When Worlds Collide

text: Why should a history account mention forced labor alongside European wealth from conquest?
answers: Some gains depended on exploiting people who did not share those benefits
All mining was freely chosen and equally rewarded
Metal cargo proves everyone became wealthy
Labor conditions are unrelated to how resources were obtained
solution: A complete explanation considers how wealth was obtained and who bore the costs. Conquest and forced labor harmed Indigenous peoples.
hint: Ask who gained resources and who was made to work.
source: NPS: Prelude to Jamestown; When Worlds Collide

text: Which item best belongs under “economic motive for exploration”?
answers: Gaining access to valuable trade goods
A chart showing possible landing places along a newly mapped coast
An astrolabe providing sky measurements during an Atlantic crossing
A magnetic compass helping the captain maintain a chosen heading
solution: Access to profitable goods is a desired economic result. Compass roses, sky angles, and steering equipment concern travel methods.
hint: A motive is something people want to achieve.
source: NPS: Prelude to Jamestown; When Worlds Collide

text: Which pair includes crops Indigenous peoples grew in the Americas before European arrival?
answers: Corn and potatoes
Wheat and barley introduced from Europe
Rice and tea associated with Asian agriculture
Olives and wheat associated with the Mediterranean
solution: Corn and potatoes were American crops that later spread widely beyond the Americas. Indigenous peoples cultivated them before European arrival.
hint: Think of foods that traveled from the Americas to Europe.
source: NPS: American Latino Theme Study: Food; Columbian Exchange

text: Which arrow correctly describes the later spread of American potatoes?
answers: Americas → Europe
Europe → Americas before Indigenous farming
Asia → Europe on Columbus’s 1492 return voyage
Europe → the Americas only after 1900
solution: Potatoes were cultivated in the Americas before they were introduced to Europe. The arrow tracks the movement asked about, not all global exchange.
hint: Start with the food’s origin, then identify the receiving region.
source: NPS: American Latino Theme Study: Food; Columbian Exchange

text: Which cargo group contains American food plants rather than navigation tools?
answers: Corn, beans, and squash
Compass, astrolabe, and a hand-drawn sailing chart
Royal banner, Bible, and a written proclamation
Silver cargo, a chart, and a magnetic compass
solution: Corn, beans, and squash are food crops with Indigenous American histories. The other lists include instruments, symbols, or metals.
hint: Separate things people grew and ate from objects used to sail.
source: NPS: American Latino Theme Study: Food; Columbian Exchange

text: A label says, “Europeans invented corn when they found the Americas.” Which correction is accurate?
answers: Indigenous peoples had cultivated corn long before European arrival
Corn was developed in Europe and first carried west by Columbus
Indigenous people began farming only after European explorers arrived
European maps are the only evidence that a crop existed before contact
solution: American crops were the result of Indigenous agricultural knowledge and cultivation. European arrival helped spread them abroad, not invent them.
hint: Distinguish growing and developing a crop from carrying it somewhere new.
source: NPS: American Latino Theme Study: Food; Columbian Exchange

text: A museum display traces tomatoes from the Americas into European cooking. What does this illustrate?
answers: The movement of foods between regions after contact
The use of American food plants to measure a ship’s latitude
The replacement of every European food crop as soon as contact occurred
The discovery that tomatoes were already a European crop before contact
solution: Tomatoes are among American crops that spread beyond the Americas. Food exchange changed what people could grow and eat.
hint: What kind of thing is moving in this display?
source: NPS: American Latino Theme Study: Food; Columbian Exchange

text: How is a sack of corn different from a compass in an exploration exhibit?
answers: Corn can be a transported food product; a compass is a navigation tool
Corn is evidence of a royal land claim; a compass is a trade product
Both objects were used mainly to estimate latitude from sky angles
A compass shows a religious motive; corn is a directional instrument
solution: The distinction is function: a food product may be carried as cargo, while a compass helps sailors travel.
hint: Classify by purpose rather than simply saying both could be aboard a ship.
source: NPS: American Latino Theme Study: Food; Columbian Exchange

text: Why should the lesson explain that foods were “new to Europeans” rather than “new to everyone”?
answers: Indigenous peoples already knew and grew those foods
Europeans were the first humans to eat food
Every American plant was created during an ocean crossing
Food could not exist without being on a European map
solution: “New” depends on whose experience is described. The crops were familiar to the Indigenous communities that cultivated and used them.
hint: Ask whose knowledge is being left out of the label.
source: NPS: American Latino Theme Study: Food; Columbian Exchange

text: A later European recipe includes potatoes, while an earlier local recipe does not. With other evidence, what change could this help illustrate?
answers: American crops became part of European diets over time
Every European household adopted potatoes on the same day
The crop must have originated in Europe because a European recipe used it
